entries.title: Disastrous Third Quarter Dooms the Mystics in Playoff Loss to Atlanta
entries.summary: Washington will host a do-or-die Game 2 on Wednesday.
entries.content:
ATLANTA — A disastrous third quarter doomed the Mystics in Game 1 of their first-round playoff series against the Dream. After leading for nearly the entirety of the first half, they unraveled after the break, ultimately losing 92-77.

They built their early lead by dominating the paint and winning the rebounding battle. Washington capably restrained Atlanta star Angel Reese, who struggled for much of the first half, starting her night by shooting 1-for-11. Making that all the more impressive was the fact that it came without much from All-Star forward Kiki Iriafen, who played less than five minutes in the opening half after picking up three quick fouls.

The Mystics still managed to stretch their lead to as many as 11 points. They were up by five when they hit the locker room. But that margin disappeared in the opening minutes of the second half.

Washington’s defense crumbled. Its offense failed to hold onto the ball. (The Mystics finished the night with 22 turnovers.) It meant they were outscored in the third quarter 29-12. They made a late push in the fourth — eventually whittling the margin to seven points with just under three minutes remaining. But the hole they had dug for themselves was simply too deep.

Sonia Citron led the Mystics in scoring with 25. Shakira Austin added 12 points and 16 rebounds. Rhyne Howard led the Dream with 26 points.

The best-of-three series moves to D.C. next. A do-or-die Game 2 for the Mystics will be held on Wednesday at 7 p.m.

entries.title: The Commanders Aren’t Done Yet, and Neither Is Terry McLaurin
entries.summary: Washington’s upset win over Seattle gives it a path back to playoff contention — and its star receiver deserves a lot of the credit.
entries.content:
There had been few things the Washington Commanders could count on through the first 11 quarters of a season already teetering on the brink of the NFL abyss before the calendar even turned to October. But on the biggest play of the young season — fourth-and-1, tie score, deep in the fourth quarter, the Commanders driving against the defending Super Bowl champions late Sunday afternoon — there was only one place for the ball to go.

At the top of the short list of sure things for the burgundy and gold is No. 17 on a simple slant route.

When veteran wideout Terry McLaurin hauled in that 5-yard pass from quarterback Marcus Mariota at Northwest Stadium, the Commanders’ season still had the faintest of heartbeats. When they kicked a field goal six plays later to take a slim lead on the Seattle Seahawks, it grew louder and steadier.

And when the final seconds ticked off their improbable, unimaginable 33-31 win — the final margin coming courtesy of linebacker Kain Medrano’s interception of a Sam Darnold pass and 50-yard return for a touchdown — that heartbeat sounded like a kick drum, threatening to burst out of the chests of every player sprinting off the Commanders’ sideline toward the celebration at the center of the field and of every waterlogged fan who endured a rainy and occasionally frustrating afternoon at the Commanders’ 2026 home opener.

“This,” McLaurin said, “was an opportunity that was seized.”

McLaurin didn’t specify whether he was speaking about himself or his team, but either interpretation would have made sense. If this was a season-saving win for the Commanders, lifting them to 1-2 ahead of their Week 4 matchup in London against the Indianapolis Colts, it was a reaffirmation for McLaurin, whose puzzling disappearance in the opening losses at Philadelphia and Dallas was beginning to raise questions about how much the eighth-year veteran had left in the tank.

“I don’t lose faith in myself, and neither do my teammates,” said McLaurin, who had six catches Sunday for 77 yards and a touchdown, his first of the season. “I know the ball is going to come my way. It’s just about being consistent and making plays. Being a part of this team where they trust me to be a leader and playmaker, I just wanted to put that on display.”

Through those first 11 quarters of their 2026 season, the Commanders had more players carted off the field with serious injuries than they had signature moments. Last week at Dallas, it was franchise quarterback Jayden Daniels riding off with a redislocated elbow that resulted in veteran backup Mariota being pressed into duty this week. And on Sunday against the Seahawks, it was linebacker Leo Chenal, carted off with a neck injury that landed him in the hospital — part of a growing injury list that still threatens to derail this team.

“It’s hard to be 0-2,” Mariota said of the hole the Commanders had dug for themselves. “It’s easy to kind of cave in this early in the year. But these guys believed in each other.”

There was nothing in the Commanders’ 2026 resume to this point that suggested anything like this was possible. They had lost 12 of their past 14 games entering Sunday, while the Seahawks had won 12 in a row, including February’s throttling of New England in the Super Bowl. Seattle was an 8 ½-point favorite on the road, which somehow seemed to undersell their talent advantage and the potency of their world-class defense, particularly against a fill-in quarterback such as Mariota.

The best decision the Commanders made all week was to make sure they involved McLaurin to a much bigger degree in their offensive attack. The two-time All-Pro came into the game with just four catches and no touchdowns on the season. Against the Eagles, he had the same number of catches (two) as run-blocking tight end John Bates, and was targeted only four times.

But on Sunday, Mariota sent the ball McLaurin’s way early and often, and early in the third quarter they connected on a 20-yard touchdown that gave the Commanders a two-touchdown lead. The play was the perfect encapsulation of why chemistry matters — and how veterans sharing the same locker room for multiple years can develop an unspoken language only they understand.

As McLaurin lined up against Seahawks cornerback Josh Jobe, he was supposed to run a 12-yard curl route.

But then — well, let McLaurin tell it:

“I beat [Jobe] so clean off the release, I ran the ‘go’ route,” he said. “Me and Marcus have enough time spent [together] to where I just trust he was going to see it, and he did. And he put the ball up where only I could get it. We don’t try to make a habit of going off-key, but we speak about being ballplayers out there, and when you get a clean release like that and you have a chance to get a big play, you want to capitalize on it.”

And all of a sudden, a season that seemed almost hopeless at the start of the weekend — with the Commanders already 0-2 in their division, having lost their starting quarterback for an undefined period, and with the defending champs arriving at Northwest Stadium — now contains a defined pathway to revived relevance.

The Commanders will travel to London as a team on Tuesday. Find a way to win there against the 1-2 Colts, and they would return to Northwest Stadium the following week at the break-even mark, with the New York Giants coming to town having lost their own quarterback, Jaxson Dart, for the season to a knee injury. At some point in there, the Commanders may even get Daniels back on the field, as he appears resolved to avoid surgery for now and is considered week to week.

The Commanders’ first-half schedule remains a beast — with clashes against the 49ers, Eagles and Rams waiting for them after the Giants game — but the back half, should they survive their early gauntlet, looks far less daunting.

The Commanders have big problems to address, particularly on the offensive line and secondary. They have an injury list that seems to grow in severity with each passing week.

But they still have No. 17, who as demonstrated on Sunday, still knows how to get into the end zone. They still have a quarterback they believe in, whether it’s Mariota or Daniels suiting up in London. And somehow, after three cathartic weeks, they still have a heartbeat.

entries.title: This Spirit Team Is Running Out of Time to Get Things Right
entries.summary: Washington lost the fifth of its last six home games this weekend and is struggling to find its form with the playoffs approaching.
entries.content:
Saturday provided the struggling Washington Spirit a rare opportunity to capture some much-needed momentum and build on last week’s 3-0 victory in Chicago. The Spirit had won back-to-back games just once since the beginning of August, a period in which they’ve labored for goals and wins alike.

That continued against Angel City FC as Washington lost its fifth home game and failed to score for the fourth time in that stretch, succumbing to a 1-0 defeat at Audi Field in D.C. An improved Spirit performance came to nothing after Angel City substitute Maiara Niehues’ long-range strike found the top corner in the 88th minute.

While the Spirit got forward and created a few half-chances, Angel City produced a moment of quality Washington couldn’t in another gut-wrenching home defeat that all but ended the Spirit’s National Women's Soccer League Shield hopes.

Washington dropped to third place with the result and, while the Spirit remain in a strong position, the team incorporating plenty of new faces admitted it is in a race against time to fix its poor form and lack of goalscoring with only four regular-season games remaining.

“It's challenging because obviously you need time to build. You bring new players, they need time to know each other, to play together, to get training sessions and also to adjust to the competition,” coach Adrián González said. “It is a process that you need time, but right now we don't have time, and we are trying to build those connections as quick as possible, knowing that we are taking risks too because we are running out of time.”

Washington (14-8-4) has earned just 10 points in nine games across August and September this season, scoring 10 goals and conceding 12 in that stretch — a far cry from what the Spirit accomplished at this stage of their last two seasons, in which they finished second and parlayed their strong form late in the year into runs to the championship game.

The Spirit went unbeaten in nine matches across August and September last year, earning 17 points, scoring 16 goals and conceding only eight in that time. Washington also finished the 2024 season strong after returning from the Olympic break, losing just two of its last 10 games.

“It's super disappointing. This used to be a fortress for us. This is a place where we take pride in being good and offering a win or a good performance for our fans,” defender Gabrielle Carle said. “I don't think this was a bad performance today. … We're struggling to score at home, but we have the talent. We have the team to do it. We just need to figure it out.”

The Spirit are in the unique situation of incorporating players who are either returning from injury or entirely new to the team into important roles so late in the season. New signing Clara Luvanga, who started training with the team on Thursday, was the latest to make her debut after coming off the bench in the 66th minute Saturday.

The Spirit's new striker showed promise, but will have very limited time to adapt to the league and her new teammates if she’s to make an instant impact this season. Washington’s sputtering offense could certainly use one, as it has struggled to produce any consistent attacking threat outside of star forward Trinity Rodman.

The Spirit have been shut out in four of their last six home games while their starting forwards have struggled. Sofia Cantore hasn’t scored or assisted in her last seven matches, since Aug. 8, while Rosemonde Kouassi has gone without a goal contribution in her last 12 Spirit games, since May 2.

The Spirit have also started a different midfield trio in six of their last seven games since Leicy Santos’ injury, although Saturday’s group of Hal Hershfelt, Andi Sullivan and Monique Ngock played well, helping the Spirit progress through Angel City’s press and advance the ball into dangerous areas.

Ngock and fellow recent midfield arrival Mélissa Bethi have produced promising moments so far, but they haven’t had much time to develop chemistry with their new teammates. That’s been exacerbated by the constant chopping and changing in midfield, which has largely been out of necessity due to injuries and suspensions.

“[We're] super excited to get those players, and they're going to be so good for us. But I think we all understand that there's a reality that we first need to learn how to play together,” Carle said. “We all want to learn together. We just have a very short window to make it work.”

Despite its recent struggles, Washington still sits third in the NWSL standings, just one point behind second-place San Diego Wave FC. Another second-place finish would ensure the Spirit home field advantage for the entirety of the playoffs, as Washington is hosting this year’s championship game.

González also said on Friday he’s hopeful Santos will be able to return soon, which would provide a massive boost. Santos scored five goals and registered four assists in 17 matches this season before her injury.

“I think it's easy to freak out, but we're doing the right things and we're creating moments. We just need to execute those,” defender Tara Rudd said. “[We’re] just trying to stay composed under pressure and really not let the outside noise get to us. We're still in a great spot on the table right now. … Hopefully that calms us down going into the next game.”

entries.title: DOJ Is Putting John Brennan in a Pinch
entries.summary: Prosecutors made the former CIA director a subject in one criminal investigation while a target of another — and it could cost them.
entries.content:
The Justice Department is squeezing former CIA Director John Brennan between two parallel criminal investigations, a strategy experts say is unorthodox and might be ill-advised, in pursuit of one of President Donald Trump’s political foes.

The DOJ subpoenaed Brennan to testify next month before a grand jury in South Florida as a “subject,” or someone under investigation but not yet accused of a crime, in a far-reaching investigation into whether Trump had his civil rights violated, his lawyer said in a court filing.

At the same time, the DOJ is actively pursuing criminal charges in the District of Columbia against Brennan as a “target,” or a likely defendant, in an investigation into allegations he lied to the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 about the Steele dossier’s role in a spy assessment about Trump-Russia matters in the 2016 election.

The dueling roles in dueling cases creates a legal minefield for Brennan to navigate, one that prosecutors could use to trip him up or create openings to charge him with a crime. Or, the strategy could end up tying prosecutors’ hands, experts said.

“What the government is doing is rather strange and makes me think: Either they don’t know what they're doing, or … it could be a Trumpian strategy to just make life as miserable and legally expensive as possible, even in cases you can't possibly win,” said Robert Weisberg, a Stanford Law School professor.

Leslie Caldwell, an attorney who oversaw the DOJ’s criminal division during the Obama administration, said of the strategy, “Unusual would be an understatement. Unprecedented would probably be a better word. And ill-advised would be an even better word.”

“It has every indicator of a classic vindictive prosecution, where the bullseye is put on certain people's heads and a desperate effort is made to gather evidence after the fact,” Caldwell told The Sun. “Those kinds of cases are generally not brought, because they're generally not good cases.”

If Brennan shows up before the grand jury next month on the grand conspiracy case, he is expected to invoke his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination — refusing to answer any questions on the stand — because of the second investigation that’s targeting him. That itself could generate headlines only a month before the midterms.

Typically, prosecutors might offer immunity against criminal charges to the subject of an investigation to compel them to testify, and doing so would all but eliminate their ability to later indict that person on related conduct.

For Brennan, that reality could tie prosecutors’ hands as they seek to investigate what Trump has alluded to as a supposedly vast conspiracy against him by former government officials who he blames for saddling his first administration with the Russia scandal in 2016, costing him reelection in 2020 and weighing down his 2024 campaign with criminal charges.

The DOJ might be willing to give up the chance to prosecute Brennan for past conduct in a bid to get him to slip up in front of the grand jury and accuse him of perjury. Steve Friedland, a law professor at Elon University in North Carolina, said grand jury testimony gives prosecutors the chance to “firm their story up,” and immunity does not protect a witness from being charged with giving false testimony.

Yet there are other possibilities, because the DOJ has deliberately situated this grand jury investigation in Fort Pierce, where a satellite courthouse at the northern edge of the Southern District of Florida has only one jurist: U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, a Trump appointee who was almost universally condemned by legal scholars over her many rulings in Trump’s Mar-a-Lago criminal case and her decision to ultimately dismiss that indictment.

FBI agents are currently exploring actions taken by former special counsel Jack Smith’s team when they prosecuted Trump for mishandling classified documents at his oceanside mansion. That creates a geographic hook for currently placing the investigation in GOP-friendly Florida — even though the West Palm Beach federal courthouse is 2.8 miles away from Mar-a-Lago while Cannon’s courthouse is 54 miles further and two counties over.

Pursuing the case at the furthest reaches of the judicial district means Cannon is in a position to resolve any disputes over Brennan’s grand jury testimony. Weisberg said prosecutors could request that Cannon privately review his testimony beforehand, and she could unilaterally decide that it doesn’t incriminate him, then force him to testify.

If Brennan still refuses to speak before the grand jury, Cannon could find him in contempt of court and send him to jail until he testifies.

And if prosecutors eventually indict Brennan in Fort Pierce, Cannon would most likely be the judge assigned to the case. That means she would also decide what to do with any defense attempt to dismiss the indictment on the grounds that prosecutors repurposed his immunized statements to go after him anyway.

Weisberg noted that prosecutors’ use of immunized statements is what led an appellate court in 1990 to overturn Oliver North’s conviction in the Iran-Contra scandal. He said any experienced prosecutor would know to tread carefully or risk hindering their ability to levy criminal charges in the future — that is, unless there’s a second objective.

It may seem odd that so much is known about an ongoing criminal investigation that hasn’t resulted in an indictment. But details have emerged in a D.C. federal lawsuit in which Brennan is asking that a judge force the DOJ to keep a record of every communication about the effort — in anticipation of a legal challenge that he “is being vindictively singled out for investigation and prosecution.”

In a declaration filed last week, defense lawyer Kenneth Wainstein detailed how Kurt Olsen — a 2020 election denier who briefly became Trump’s White House election czar and is now at the DOJ — recently informed him on a call with the prosecution team that there are several “viable” grand jury investigations.

U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb held a hearing last week on the matter but has yet to issue a ruling.

Trump has spent years publicly vowing to exact revenge on Brennan, Smith and a long list of other current and former government officials, including his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg, one-time Jan. 6 Committee Chair Liz Cheney, former FBI director James Comey, New York Attorney General Letitia James, former President Barack Obama, recently departed Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, Sen. Adam Schiff of California, and others.

Earlier this month, Joseph diGenova, the MAGA loyalist who oversaw a Florida-based investigation, quit as counselor to the attorney general.

DiGenova had publicly accused Brennan of being a “real traitor” and had already advocated for a criminal prosecution of the former CIA director before joining the investigation. His appointment to the DOJ role followed the removal from the prosecution team of career national security prosecutor Maria Medetis Long, who raised concerns about a rushed effort to bring charges against Brennan.

Concerns that diGenova had been “slow rolling” the investigation may have played a role in his abrupt departure, the New York Post reported. He denied allegations that he had lost focus in an interview with the newspaper.

“If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem,” diGenova told the Post.

entries.title: All-DMV High School Football Players of Week 5
entries.summary: This weekend’s standouts include a dominant defensive end from Churchill and a running back who produced video game-like numbers from Lake Braddock.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. Every week, we’ll have a volleyball players of the week story on Wednesday, and boys and girls soccer selections Friday. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here. 

It’s hard to believe that for some DMV football programs, the regular season is nearly halfway complete. In another strong week of local football, here’s who stood out the most to earn All-DMV Player of the Week:

John Lafontant, Senior, Linebacker, Coolidge

Lafontant shined on both sides of the ball for the Colts in Friday’s blowout 43-0 win over Bell. He was a constant disruption at linebacker for coach Kevin Nesbitt’s team, racking up 12 tackles including three tackles for loss and a forced fumble. He also rushed for 97 yards and a touchdown on offense as Coolidge earned its second-straight victory.

Saahir Lester, Senior, Defensive End, Churchill

When Lester first started playing football for Churchill, he was a 135-pound underclassman insistent on playing the defensive end position. Now a senior, Lester has blossomed into a 210-pound force along the edge for the undefeated Bulldogs. Last week against Whitman, he accounted for three tackles for loss, two sacks and a forced fumble as Churchill downed the Vikings, 35-14.

Dylan Miller, Senior, Quarterback, South County

Miller put together an efficient performance to quarterback the Stallions to an impressive 31-21 victory over district rival West Springfield. Miller threw for 325 yards and three passing touchdowns as South County moved to 3-1 on the season. Miller’s third touchdown was the cherry on top of his dominant day — he fired a 33-yard strike on fourth-and-13 to give his team a comfortable two-score advantage with just minutes left in the fourth quarter.

Sam Rhye, Senior, Running Back, Lake Braddock

Rhye is the heartbeat of a Lake Braddock offense that dropped 35 points in a big win over Robinson. The run-heavy Bruins handed the ball to their star senior 25 times in the 35-21 victory — Rhye rushed for 241 yards and four touchdowns. His final carry of the evening, a 49-yard burst on fourth-and-1, iced the game to give Lake Braddock its second-straight win.

Ethan Stanford, Senior, Linebacker, Bishop McNamara

Bishop McNamara’s defense put together a sterling defensive performance on a rainy Saturday afternoon against Washington Catholic Athletic Conference rival Archbishop Carroll. Stanford, the team’s standout linebacker, was at the center of it all. The senior finished with 10 tackles, including one for loss as the Mustangs held the Lions to just six points in a 20-6 victory. Coach Greg Calhoun will continue to rely on Stanford to make plays with conference matchups against Gonzaga, DeMatha, St. John’s and Good Counsel looming in October and November.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Crash Course
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 28, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Driverless car crashes, no verdict for Trayon White and MYSTICS TBD.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit: 7/10. Mainly bright but breezy. Still, it’s plenty comfortable with temperatures up a handful of degrees from yesterday. Full forecast from Capital Weather.

THE LATEST

Autonomous vehicles have been test-driving around D.C. for years. DDOT won’t share how many times they’ve crashed.

The city has a rule against sharing AV-involved crash incidents through public records requests and hasn’t published the reports it promised to with that information. Federal data shows that AVs have been involved in 15 crashes in D.C. from July 2021 to August 2026, The Washington Sun’s Zara Norman reports.

Waymo — the U.S.’s largest AV company — reached out to The Sun to confirm that it has logged seven crash incidents since it began testing in 2024, with three minor injuries and three instances of property damage reported. Most of the events involved other drivers rear-ending Waymos while they slowed or stopped for traffic, or yielded to emergency vehicles, according to a spokesperson.

But only six of Waymo’s seven disclosed incidents show up on that federal database, which requires crashes to meet a certain reporting threshold, meaning that it is not a full accounting. The Sun has appealed to the mayor’s office for the city’s complete set of records ahead of the council’s vote this fall on whether to permit AVs here.

“The current mayoral administration has done little to move forward with the responsible deployment of fully autonomous vehicles, making it impossible for Washingtonians to benefit from the technology or understand how it is performing on their roads,” a Waymo spokesperson told The Sun.

Ward 6 council member Charles Allen, who chairs D.C.’s transportation committee, said his legislation allowing AVs would override the city’s statute barring the sharing of crash safety data and require companies to regularly disclose any incidents as well as other data points.

“There’s a value in proactively reporting information,” Allen told The Sun.





FROM THE COURTHOUSE

There’s still no verdict in the Trayon White bribery trial, The Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports. Jurors, who began deliberations on Wednesday, told U.S. District Judge Rudolph Contreras on Friday morning that they were unable to reach a unanimous conclusion as to White’s guilt or innocence.

White’s defense asked Contreras to declare a mistrial. Contreras said “in the grand scheme of things, it hasn’t been that long” and told the jury to keep trying. “I know it’s a difficult statute,” he said, referring to the law on bribery.

Prosecutors allege that the Ward 8 council member accepted illegal bribes in exchange for agreeing to help a D.C. contractor secure government contracts for anti-violence work. The contractor who paid White was working as an FBI informant, allowing authorities to secretly record his conversations with White during the summer of 2024.

White’s defense argued that while the lawmaker did accept $35,000 in cash payments from the contractor, he never actually intended to pressure government officials to extend those contracts. Some D.C. government officials testified that White had asked them about the contractor’s company, but none told the jury that White had actually pressured them or influenced the award process.

In order to prove that White committed bribery, prosecutors had to show that White actually intended to be influenced by the money that the informant gave him.

So what was White’s intention? The jury is clearly still out.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Power Hour: Hundreds gathered at a bitcoin-themed bar in D.C. this weekend to celebrate data centers, denouncing “bipartisan psychosis” around artificial intelligence over Loudoun County Iced Teas, The Sun’s Mara Hoplamazian and Emily Kennard report.

Kennedy Center officials were long aware of the structural issues they blamed for the storied arts building’s closure this month and delayed repairs, a group of anonymous former employees wrote in a letter to Congress, the Associated Press reports.

Lanes closures in the 9th Street Tunnel begin today, as part of construction that isn’t expected to be completed until June, WTOP reports.





FROM THE DINING ROOM

Tom Sietsema, The Sun’s food correspondent, dishes on a “deal of a meal.”

Earlier this month, the cozy Masala Art in Washington’s Tenleytown started serving thalis for lunch on Friday. I’m talking four small dishes — plus cooling raita, naan, rice and dessert — for a mere $22. Better yet, diners can choose from a meat or vegetarian sampler. The selections might include smoky mashed eggplant and grilled paneer tikka masala among the vegetable dishes and lamb korma and chicken tikka masala among the meaty items.

I admire the presentation as much as the food, which is “chef’s choice,” says owner Atul Bhola of the freshly made, ever-changing lineup. The dishes are set on little plates atop a semi-circular copper tray, one per grazer. It’s a lot of style for not a lot of dough. And it fills a wish for those who crave variety.

“It’s a buffet on your table,” says Bhola, who adds that second helpings are part of the bargain.





FROM “PERSPECTIVES”

It was once very cool to be super into “Hamilton,” then it got uncool, The Sun’s Anusha Mathur writes for our “Perspectives” section. Elanna Bellofatto, a spin class instructor in D.C., is staging a comeback with themed sessions inspired by the hit musical. Yes, she wears the wig.

“Perspectives” is The Sun’s platform for analysis, ideas and narratives.





TRIVIA


Who is the only U.S. president to attend college in D.C.?

  1. Bill Clinton
  2. Woodrow Wilson
  3. Jimmy Carter
Email us your answer — the first reader who gets it right will receive a shout-out at the end of tomorrow’s newsletter.





SPORTS

A disastrous third quarter doomed the Mystics in Game 1 of their first-round playoff series against the Dream, The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri reports from Atlanta. After leading for nearly the entire first half, they unraveled after the break, ultimately losing 92-77. The Mystics will host a do-or-die Game 2 on Wednesday.

The Commanders are back from the dead, metaphorically speaking, after stunning the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks yesterday, 33-31. With the win, and injured star QB Jayden Daniels being labeled week-to-week as opposed to done for the year following his gruesome elbow injury last week, there’s reason to believe this Commanders season could actually mean something, The Sun’s Dave Sheinin writes.




Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Jeff Dooley and Gaby Morera Di Núbila.

entries.title: The Washington Sun: The White House App Is Watching You
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The privacy cost of Trump TV. Parts of MAGA reel over the China summit. John Brennan’s parallel legal woes. The GOP’s Senate plan that’s gone sideways. And: The AI bros celebrate data centers.

THE LATEST

The White House app got very popular as the administration launched its own 24/7 stream amid Donald Trump’s newest effort to choose who gets to cover him. Social media channels teased “something’s coming” in the lead up to the launch of Trump TV, and that something came with a hefty privacy price.

The White House app covertly collects excessive user data and shares it with third-party trackers while sidestepping federal security rules, The Washington Sun’s Gavin J. Quinton reports. For example, the app includes scripts to monitor a user’s location several times per minute.

While networks halted their pool coverage in solidarity with the White House’s banned media outlets, the Trump administration heralded the app as a legitimate source for news.

“The people who do want to hear that message are going to the White House for it, and in doing so, they're giving up a lot of information about themselves, and that provides the White House with an advantage going into the midterms,” Philip Fields, a cybersecurity researcher and former FBI intelligence analyst who has researched the app, told Gavin.

Cybersecurity experts have tried to sound the alarm about the app since its release in March, and pushback over its security forced White House developers to delegate tracking software to third-party services.

The app is already preloaded on government-furnished mobile devices across the executive branch and has more than 2 million downloads, but where the user data ends up and what it’s being used for remains a mystery. The White House did not respond to requests for comment and left its app-store-required “privacy manifest” completely blank — implying it collects no data from users despite contradicting findings from cybersecurity experts.

“The bottom line is this app is just not very stable or secure,” said Joseph Gera, a former Apple App Store developer and senior platform engineer. “It's asking for your location data in real time. It also asks for personal information to access your financial data, to access your messages, to access all kinds of information.”

FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


MAGA vs. MAGA on China visit: “It is astonishing what is going on right now — Trump is functionally a China dove right now,” a Trump administration ally told The Sun, illustrating the thinking of a cadre of Trump supporters who were enraged by the optics of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit last week. Our Jeff Stein reports those disaffected, including Steve Bannon and Laura Loomer, are going public with their concerns, and voicing them privately to the White House.

Surprisingly, Peter Navarro, one of the most vocal China hawks in the president’s orbit, defended the red carpets, fawning toasts and blue ribbon tour of D.C. as part of a consistent strategy to pressure China. “Frequent one-on-one meetings allow POTUS to express obvious concern and at times displeasure with promises made but unkept, and this helps keep things on track,” he told The Sun in a statement.

entries.title: White House Drove Users to Official App Fraught With Trackers
entries.summary: The White House app became the App Store’s most downloaded news app after the president barred three news outlets.
entries.content:
The White House app shot to the top of the Apple App Store’s news category last week after its new 24/7 broadcast channel, Trump TV, was swiftly positioned as a legitimate source for news while networks halted their pool coverage.

“The American people are not waiting on those cameras; they are going straight to the Presidency,” the White House said in a news release heralding the app, which hosts the Trump TV stream.

In order to see that messaging, users have to give something in exchange: their data. And they have no idea what the government could do with it.

“The people who do want to hear that message are going to the White House for it, and in doing so, they're giving up a lot of information about themselves, and that provides the White House with an advantage going into the midterms,” said Philip Fields, a cybersecurity researcher and former FBI intelligence analyst who has researched the app.

Experts have speculated the data, including the results of political polling hosted by the app, could be used to push campaign messaging onto users, or to report a user to Immigration and Customs Enforcement or the Secret Service. Some think it could be used to make money.

No one can say definitively where the user data ends up. But it’s clear the White House app covertly collects excessive user data and shares it with third-party trackers while sidestepping federal security rules, according to cybersecurity experts and an independent risk assessment conducted by The Washington Sun.

“The bottom line is this app is just not very stable or secure,” said Joseph Gera, a former Apple App Store developer and senior platform engineer. “It's asking for your location data in real time. It also asks for personal information to access your financial data, to access your messages, to access all kinds of information.”

Federal apps and websites are required to meet federal security requirements designed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology and authorized by security experts within each agency.

The White House declined to comment on multiple questions, including whether its app meets the high standard of federal risk management frameworks, instead referring The Washington Sun to its news release promoting the app’s success.

The White House app drew scrutiny earlier this year over a host of cybersecurity issues that analysts said make data vulnerable for both users and government staffers by regularly sharing their IP addresses, time zones and other data to third-party services like Parsely, OneSignal and a Russian widget service called Elfsight.

Despite those issues, the app remains preloaded on government-furnished mobile devices across the executive branch. After the Trump administration mandated that federal agencies force-install the app onto all government-issued mobile devices, cybersecurity researchers noted that no public security authorization or privacy assessments required under federal law had been completed.

Pushback over the app’s security apparatus forced White House developers to delegate tracking software to third-party services. But the app still includes scripts to monitor a user’s location several times per minute, according to Gera, and it’s unclear how that data is used by the White House or third-party services.

“The way that they're doing their collection now is harder to discern, because they've just used commercial trackers instead,” Fields said.

The app also contains a latent keylogger script sourced online from an amateur developer based in India, according to Gera and confirmed by The Sun’s analysis. Keyloggers most commonly appear in surveillance malware to store written text from a device, but they also can be used as a benign tool to analyze inputs like typing frequency. While it’s unlikely to work on mobile devices, Fields said, it’s still concerning that the White House is using a keylogger web-sourced from an foreign coder.

According to internal app files, the software was developed by 45Press, a self-purported WordPress developer based in Ohio. Public contracts show the company was awarded more than $1.4 million in February to support the White House’s online services. 45Press does not directly answer questions from the media regarding customer contracts.

App marketplaces require developers to disclose what data app developers collect from their users, which platforms like the Apple App Store enforce through a “privacy manifest.”

In the app’s latest version, the White House left that manifest completely blank, implying it collects no data from users despite contradicting findings from cybersecurity experts.

Data collected through the app is sent primarily to a host of third-party service providers, who may sell it to advertisers, state adversaries or back to the federal government, Fields said, adding that federal agencies have admitted to purchasing Americans’ information from data brokers.

“It could be bought and sold by government agencies at this point because they've decided that they're not going to take the Carpenter ruling seriously,” he said. “And they can just go and get ad data for free from the private sector or buy it from them without legal process.”

The Supreme Court ruled in Carpenter v. United States that federal agencies cannot obtain cellphone location data without a warrant.

Federal agencies have gone around the ruling by claiming data sourced from brokers is anonymous and is tied to mobile advertising IDs instead of a name. Experts have pushed back on that claim, arguing that device location data — like home and workplace addresses and commute patterns — make it possible to connect an advertising ID with a person’s real identity, especially when coupled with advanced artificial intelligence tools.

The White House app’s privacy policy explicitly states that data collected “is governed by the third-party website’s security and privacy policies.” It adds that user data can be used to create tailored content and statistical profiles for users, inform policy decisions, or share “information with other government agencies in response to lawful law enforcement requests.”

An unpublished feature within the White House browser extension allowed app administrators to create a political profile on a user, and included an “investigate” button to refer individuals to the Secret Service.

The Trump administration has made a concerted effort to repurpose Americans’ sensitive personal information in consolidated federal databases, according to the Center for American Progress. In an August report, a CAP tech policy analyst detailed how the administration has shared taxpayer and Medicaid records with ICE officials amid DOGE’s push to combine agency records.

“Centralized databases are also more vulnerable to security breaches and internal misuse,” the report states.

In 2015, the Office of Personnel Management suffered a catastrophic data breach that compromised security clearance data of 21 million federal employees and contractors.

One of those employees was Peter Loge, a former Obama-appointed advisor at the Food and Drug Administration who now leads the Project on Ethics in Political Communication at George Washington University.

Loge contends that rather than using user data for political strategy, the White House is more likely to leverage the information to steer supporters driven to the app toward one of Trump’s merchandise or cryptocurrency ventures.

“What we’ve seen is that Donald Trump is a businessman who's monetizing politics. Therefore, this app is a way to make money,” Loge said. “The other people who could find this information either directly or through several layers of resale are, of course, hostile governments — foreign actors whose interests are the demise of American democracy.”

entries.title: ‘No One Feels Good’: Republicans' Senate Map Keeps Getting Worse
entries.summary: Republicans are starting to see trouble in red states they never imagined they’d lose and giving up on states they were fighting for.
entries.content:
The path for Republicans to keep their Senate majority is getting smaller by the day — a once-unthinkable prospect for the party.

Republican members for months have acknowledged that rising gas prices and other costs, largely stemming from the Iran war, are a massive problem, especially for their electoral prospects. That talk finally hit reality in recent days as the bottom fell out of polls in a number of states.

Republicans are breaking with President Donald Trump, big ad buys are being canceled, several solidly red states are starting to look shaky, and piles of money are being diverted to places where Republicans were hoping they wouldn’t have to spend.

“Six months ago, the reaction was sort of, ‘Eh, we've got problems with the Republicans, and they're not perfect, but the other side's crazy now,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) told The Washington Sun. “Now, it's more like, ‘Both sides are crazy.’”

“The people are upset about the cost of living and they're confused about Iran,” Kennedy said, adding multiple times that the election is going to be “close.”

Republicans earlier this year had a straightforward view of the midterms. The plan was to compete and limit damage in a trio of battleground states (Georgia, North Carolina and Maine), while successfully playing defense in Republican territory and limiting big spends where they didn’t have to.

That plan is going sideways. The Georgia race, between Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and GOP Rep. Mike Collins has fallen further out of the Republican column, with the Cook Political Report rating the contest as “Likely Democrat” last week.

In North Carolina, a top outside super PAC last week canceled $6.5 million in ad spending to back Republican Michael Whatley, who is badly trailing former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper — an indication the group didn’t believe the money would have moved the needle in Whatley’s direction.

“It’s very difficult for a Republican to win statewide,” said the state’s retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, adding that Whatley has done little to differentiate himself from the overall GOP brand. “Right now, his work is to go after the unaffiliated and having some separation. I don’t see any evidence of separation between [Whatley] and the president.”

Republicans expect more dollar slashing in the two states in the near future in order to shore up support elsewhere, despite the party’s sizable financial advantage.

“Those candidates have [had] their chances,” one Republican operative working on Senate races said, noting the big money spent in both states in recent months and that the numbers have remained largely unchanged. “Time to go find other races.”

In Maine, the race between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson is neck-and-neck, with public polls showing each holding a small lead. Collins has found herself on the defensive after a ProPublica report accused her of taking part in a pay-to-play scheme involving a convicted defense contractor. She has vigorously denied the allegations.

However, Republicans have made some progress defining Jackson, with 47 percent viewing him unfavorably — a number that has ticked up by 15 percentage points since late July after heavy spending by outside groups.

But Republicans now have turned their attention to a foursome of red states that are likely to determine who controls the upper chamber next year. It’s a position they didn’t expect to be in.

Ohio and Alaska are atop that list. Both feature incumbents who are facing headwinds that are proving difficult to overcome.

Republican Sen. Jon Husted is playing defense on numerous fronts against former Sen. Sherrod Brown. Brown has repeatedly gone after Husted’s support for data centers during his tenure as lieutenant governor, with Brown labeling him “the face of data centers” in Ohio.

In a sign of the trouble Husted faces, the Senate will stay in town for the coming week, in part to vote on a bill aimed at having tech companies cover data center-driven energy costs.

The race is quickly becoming a money pit for both parties, with over $300 million pouring into the state between past and future ad spending, according to AdImpact.

Public polls have shown Brown leading by 4 percentage points — a margin similar to the advantage he held against Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno two years ago. Moreno ended up defeating him by 3.5 percentage points.

The question is whether the polling drop-off experienced in other states is indicative of the coming final result or if Republicans just aren’t paying attention yet and will vote GOP when it counts. One Republican operative with Ohio ties argued that the sudden downturn in the numbers is similar to what the party experienced around the 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic — but adding that they don’t believe high prices and the war are yet to the point they’d see 2008 or 2020-like results.

“We’ve been through two massive economic shocks in the last 20 years,” the operative with Ohio ties said. “We know what those things look like, right? Does this feel like one of those right now?”

“It’s bad out there. No one feels good,” conceded one senior Senate Republican aide. “But there’s still time for things to improve.”

For Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), the dynamics are even worse than elsewhere on the map. Gas prices are eclipsing $5 a gallon and diesel costs are hovering around $6.70 a gallon — both higher than the national average.

Far-flung parts of the state are being hit even harder. Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) noted the price in one key fishing area was $12.99 gallon.

“People are feeling it, and they don’t like it. They don’t like it at all,” Murkowski recently told reporters.

Alaska is hard for operatives to wrap their arms around due to the state’s ranked-choice voter system and the difficulty of polling in Alaska, leaving them largely in the dark until voters actually go to the polls.

Texas and Iowa round out the quartet, with Republicans showing signs of being rattled in both states despite continued hope that each ultimately will fall into their column. But it’s going to cost them.

In Texas, the battle between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico has forced the party in power to spend heavily to pull the race back into their column. A top super PAC aligned with the Senate Leadership Fund has booked $117 million in past and future ad spending — a number that is expected to increase.

Republicans argued earlier this year that backing Sen. John Cornyn over Paxton would have avoided this exact scenario, which is forcing the party to spend heavily when it may not have needed to otherwise.

“There's a limited resource, and I think at some point, you know, the powers that be are going to have to make decisions about where you spend money, and if you spend it for lost causes in some of these places that aren't looking good, should you move that money to places where it might make a difference,” Cornyn told reporters last week. When asked if Paxton is a lost cause, Cornyn responded. “I'm going to leave that up to the voters.”

Like Cornyn, the party is not oozing with confidence. One Texas-based Republican strategist told The Sun that they view the race as a 50-50 proposition, after having said in mid-August that they believed it was 60-40 in Paxton’s favor.

In Iowa, polls shifted against Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson in her race against Democrat Josh Turek, showing them in a toss-up. Weeks after voting against a war powers resolution, Hinson called for an end to the Iran conflict, citing sky-high gas prices in her state.

The news gets worse from there. Some in the party are fretting that they’ve had to spend time and resources in Kansas to defend Sen. Roger Marshall’s seat.

A first-term member, Marshall has been under siege over his purported lack of ties to the state. The concern has led outside groups to spend seven-figure amounts to boost him, with Vice President JD Vance recently stopping in the state for an event. Republicans admit that months ago, Kansas wasn’t anywhere near their radar.

“I would’ve said that doesn’t sound right,” said Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia).

Republicans have also talked up their chances in New Hampshire and Michigan as possible flip opportunities, though both could be tall tasks. Operatives believe New Hampshire is the more likely of the two to go red, given Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s sizable polling advantage in her reelection campaign.

Overall, Republicans believe the avenue to keeping their majority exists — but few are thrilled with how things are playing out.

“Is it a shitty environment? Absolutely. Does it seem to be getting worse? Absolutely,” a second Republican operative involved in Senate races said. “Is it possible to keep the majority? It’s still possible.”

entries.title: The Commanders Are Bringing Back Austin Ekeler
entries.summary: The 31-year-old running back played for Washington in 2024 and 2025.
entries.content:
The Commanders are bringing back a familiar face to help bolster their backfield.

On Monday, the NFL Network reported that the Commanders are expected to sign free agent running back Austin Ekeler, who played for the team during the 2024 and 2025 seasons.

The 31-year-old joins a Washington running back room that’s been led by Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White through three games. Croskey-Merritt is averaging just 3 yards per carry as the Commanders primary ball carrier (although he did have a long touchdown run wiped out by a penalty Sunday against Seattle), while White has been used more frequently as a receiver out of the backfield.

When healthy, Ekeler is one of the NFL’s better all-purpose running backs. Undrafted out of Division II Western Colorado in 2017, Ekeler led the NFL in touchdowns in 2021 and 2022, with 18 and 20, respectively, with a strong mix of scoring as a running back and pass-catcher. After playing for the Chargers from 2017 to 2023, Ekeler signed a two-year contract with the Commanders in 2024.

He earned All-Pro honors as a kick returner with the Commanders in 2024, but tore his Achilles in the second week of the 2025 season. Ekeler worked out for the Panthers last week, according to the NFL Network, but chose to reunite with the Commanders instead.

Ekeler’s signing comes a day after the Commanders shocked the reigning champion Seahawks, 33-31, with backup quarterback Marcus Mariota filling in for the injured Jayden Daniels. The team heads to London to face the Colts next Sunday in a game that will kick off at 9:30 a.m. ET.

entries.title: The Nats Took a Step Forward This Year. Fans Still Deserve More.
entries.summary: It is nearly impossible to judge this Nationals season, which came to a conclusion on Sunday, within the binary of good or bad.
entries.content:
Now this is the part where, based on interviews, my observations and some cherry-picked statistics, I’m supposed to tell you if the Washington Nationals overachieved or underachieved in 2026. We like to boil our sports down to binaries like that, the most popular one, of course, also being the most elemental: Did the team win, or did it lose? Let’s begin, then, with that test.

These Nationals, as we knew them, lost on two basic levels. They finished with more losses (85) than wins (77), ending the year with a 6-4 victory over the Mets on Sunday. And, starting Tuesday, almost half the league will compete in the playoffs, and they will not. That has been the case for seven years running, for every season since they won the World Series in 2019. It’s worn on the fan base, which is not, it turns out, something you just have to trust me on. The total attendance for the year, 1,839,116, was the lowest for any post-title season not affected by the pandemic. Social media may be the fastest way to poll a team’s popularity (or lack thereof). A way better measure, though, is when fans stop opening their wallets.

But like with most things outside of the actual games, it is hard — impossible, even — to judge this year within the binary of good or bad. The bullpen, if you hadn’t heard, was definitionally bad, blowing 42 saves, five more than the previous MLB record. By contrast, the offense was all kinds of good, scoring more runs than every team but the Cubs and Brewers, who are both in the playoffs.

Those extremes are probably the best way to distill the central tension of the season. It is fair to say that, by spending very, very, very little on an obvious weakness last winter, the Nats wasted the kind of offensive performance that may not come back around for a while, even when (or if) the Lerner family decides to run a competitive payroll again. And yet, after Vegas had the Nationals winning about 65 games, they comfortably beat that projection because the offense was so ahead of schedule — a credit to the players, yes, but importantly the new coaching staff, too.

No one’s ever hung a banner for talking about bat speed and launch angle more. But after most of the front office and staff turned over, talking about bat speed and launch angle more was clearly a necessary start. The new regime also sped up their own honeymoon period by leading the team to a surprising amount of success in the first four months of the season. They’re facing real expectations sooner than expected, which is almost always better than the alternative.

“We haven't experienced what it's been like over the course of the last five years here, six years, whatever it is,” Paul Toboni, the Nats’ first-year president of baseball operations, said in his end-of-season address Friday. “And my guess is that it might just be a feeling of: ‘Hey, we’re in September and we’re out of it. Let's just look forward to the season ending.’ And we were very, very adamant about that not being the energy in the clubhouse.”

“We would send messages like: ‘We have to carry out the day like we are tied or a game back in the wild card, even though we're not, even though we're six, seven out, whatever it is. Because at some point here in the near future we are going to be tied for the wild card or a couple games up, or whatever it might be, and I don't want the feeling to be foreign to them.”

On Friday, ahead of the last series of the season, manager Blake Butera said that if the Nats had just an average bullpen this year, they’d have probably made the playoffs. It was a self-aware quote that may also be tough for fans to read, especially given how fast the team faded after trading Curtis Mead, Luis García Jr. and Foster Griffin at the deadline, making for an August and September that looked and felt too familiar. Once again, it was all in service of the future, which is rarely said when the present is going well. But now that we’ve dipped into the overplayed coping mechanisms, what’s the harm in a little more?

On Saturday, in the AAA national championship game in Las Vegas, Jarlin Susana, one of the Nats’ top prospects, threw the hardest pitch of the AAA season, a 104-mph fastball. Never mind that the Rochester Red Wings, the Nationals’ AAA affiliate, lost after … blowing a save, then allowing three runs in the tenth. There was a 104-mph fastball! And on top of that, all 17 of Susana’s heaters were clocked at at least 101.5 mph. The pitch averaged 102.8 for two innings. We can easily apply the binary in this case: That is good!

Susana, 22, joined the organization as part of the return for Juan Soto four summers ago. He’s among the minor leaguers who could really help the Nats in the near future, to say nothing of the blue-chip hitters a bit farther away, starting with Eli Willits, the first pick in the 2025 draft, and Chris Hacopian, the 11th pick in 2026. When Toboni took over as the Nationals’ big boss, he said he wanted to build a “scouting and player development monster.” At the very least, with staffing and messaging alone, the Nats seem to be on a much better track to that than they were this time last year. That’s a point toward calling the year a success.

“The farm system, I think for the most part there have been a bunch of great strides there,” Toboni said. “But I think like most things in this game, that's pretty fragile and doesn't necessarily mean that those strides are going to continue into the future if we don't really stay on it. So there's like this probably underlying sense of … I'm not a very anxious person, but anxiety like: We got to keep pushing forward because we're not where we want to be.”

Then on Sunday, Andrés Chaparro, one of the Nats’ platoon first basemen, launched two home runs to cap a breakout second half. Out of the bullpen, Will Dion, Riley Cornelio, Jack Sinclair and Erik Tolman, none of whom were on the Opening Day roster, combined to pitch six scoreless innings. The season confirmed that James Wood, Cade Cavalli, CJ Abrams and Daylen Lile are the major league players most capable of headlining the next winning team in D.C. But to that end, even a hint of some supporting characters felt like incremental progress. Chaparro should get a shot to keep proving himself next season (whenever that begins, given the high potential for a lockout in the coming months). And in Tolman, a homegrown pitcher who came all the way back from a gruesome leg injury, the staff sees the outline of a high-leverage reliever.

But here’s the thing about discussing the Nats this way, about still putting more stock in what could happen than what is happening: It’s old. Whenever we’re viewing the Nationals from 30,000 feet, it’s worth recycling the idea that the new front office was tasked with building a sustainable winner, not rushing their process because of how bleak the past half decade has been. That means not discounting their wins, incremental or otherwise, because of how stale the act of looking to the future has gotten. For the time being, for at least a little longer, that feels logical, fair.

Yet on the other hand, something has to give for this fan base. And soon, too, to once again recognize the social contract between a team and its city. Nats fans deserve to actually watch a competitive core instead of projecting one. They deserve, as a reciprocation for spending on tickets, a television package and merchandise, for ownership to invest in a club that could reach the postseason one of these years. The labor battle could be a complicating factor for immediate plans with the roster and payroll. But it doesn’t make any of that less true.

entries.title: U.S. Navy Warship Faced ‘Critical Threat of Mechanical Failure’: Documents
entries.summary: Problems with the USS Santa Barbara risked crew safety and invited "catastrophic flooding," according to a government contracting request.
entries.content:
The newly commissioned USS Santa Barbara has already seen better days.

The Navy’s 418-foot littoral combat vessel experienced serious maintenance issues that plagued it in the weeks before it arrived earlier this month in a Singapore port, according to an undated government contracting document reviewed by The Washington Sun.

“All four engines are currently operating well beyond their maximum recommended operational thresholds, presenting an immediate, critical threat of mechanical failure,” the document states.

Maintenance on the two main propulsion diesel engines and two of the diesel generators that power the ship was “urgently required to prevent catastrophic engine failure, preserve vessel operational readiness, and ensure crew safety,” the contracting document states. The need for critical repairs on the ship comes as the Navy is strained by operational issues stemming from the Iran war, such as the USS Abraham Lincoln’s overextended deployment.

A Navy spokesperson referred questions to the 7th Fleet.

In a statement to The Sun, 7th Fleet Deputy Public Affairs Officer Cody Milam said: “We can confirm that the USS Santa Barbara (LCS 32) safely arrived in Singapore for a repair availability to address required maintenance. Forward-deployed maintenance is standard practice, and upon completion of these repairs, the ship will continue supporting fleet and combatant commander tasking in the region.”

The Navy commissioned the USS Santa Barbara — ship motto: “Resilient and Determined” — in 2023. The ship deployed from San Diego in early 2025. It spent time in the Persian Gulf last year and is now on deployment with the 7th Fleet in the Indo-Pacific.

Last month, it took part in a seven day joint exercise with the Royal Australian Navy and Philippine Navy in the Philippine Exclusive Economic Zone. The exercise was a success, but not all was well with the ship.

The USS Santa Barbara was already slated for routine maintenance at the Sembawang Wharves port in Singapore starting Sept. 4, but the Navy struggled to find contractors who could carry out additional fixes needed aboard the vessel, documents show.

A routine maintenance contract was awarded to Epsilon Systems Solutions Inc. on Aug. 6, and the company was awarded the additional engine maintenance as a “logical follow-on” to its existing contract.

But when the Navy put out a call in August to a dozen of its contractors for a separate slate of needed repairs, it received zero bids, leaving the government to rely on local Singaporean facilities that have standing agreements with the Navy.

The additional ship repairs include the replacement of two of the ship’s service diesel generators’ raw water cooling pumps and a separate fire pump, the “non-operational” status of which “severely compromises shipboard firefighting capability.”

The ship also needed a new stern tube seal.

“Failure to execute this replacement before underway operations invites catastrophic flooding risks,” one of the documents reads.

The selected local contractor was not disclosed in the Navy documents, which show the limited-source contract was justified under a federal statute allowing “unusual and compelling urgency.”

Last week, the Navy relied on the USS Canberra, another littoral combat vessel that launched alongside the USS Santa Barbara, for an exercise with the Republic of Singapore Navy in the South China Sea.

Littoral combat ships are a relatively new kind of Navy warship, smaller than a destroyer and designed to operate near shorelines.

“Preparing our ships and crews is a full team effort,” Milam’s statement continued. “By working with partners across government and industry, we ensure our warships remain ready to support security and stability throughout the Indo-Pacific."

entries.title: Florida AG Asks a Judge to Stop OpenAI From Developing New Models
entries.summary: “Stop calling it safe. Stop pretending it’s human. Stop selling it to kids,” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said.
entries.content:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is asking a judge to bar OpenAI from developing new artificial intelligence models without independent safety approval, escalating its lawsuit against the company and CEO Sam Altman.

“Today, we ask the court for a new temporary injunction. No new model development without independent safety guardrails,” Uthmeier said in a video announcing the request Monday.

The motion, filed in Highlands County Circuit Court, also asks the judge to bar minors from using ChatGPT and restrict OpenAI’s collection of data from children under 13 without specified parental protections. It seeks to prohibit the company from claiming ChatGPT is safe or reliable, giving the chatbot human attributes and using tactics to prolong conversations.

“Stop calling it safe. Stop pretending it’s human. Stop selling it to kids,” Uthmeier said in the video, arguing that evidence of safety failures had grown since Florida sued OpenAI in June.

The motion cites several recent incidents in which OpenAI models allegedly bypassed safeguards, including a July breach of open-source AI repository Hugging Face during an OpenAI cybersecurity evaluation. It also points to attempted hacks of U.S. government websites and an incident in which an OpenAI agent accessed an Australian government health department website without authorization.

The filing also quotes OpenAI board member Paul Christiano’s recent warning of a “meaningful risk” of catastrophic loss of control, and cites a report that OpenAI, Anthropic and outside researchers are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving AI models behaving in ways evaluators considered problematic.

Florida sued OpenAI and Altman in June, alleging the company misrepresented ChatGPT’s safety and exposed users, including children, to harm. OpenAI moved the case to federal court, but the judge granted Florida’s request to return it to state court earlier this month.

OpenAI separately said Monday that it had paused training on its most capable models and would resume only after adding safeguards and alignment improvements.

“If Sam Altman meant what he said about slowing down, he can join our ask to the court,” Uthmeier said in his video. “If he will not, we ask the court to do what OpenAI will not do for itself: protect Florida families.”

entries.title: Jasmine Crockett Snubs Talarico in New List of Endorsements
entries.summary: Crockett had committed to focusing on “down-ballot” candidates in Texas instead of joining Talarico on the campaign trail.
entries.content:
Rep. Jasmine Crockett’s leadership PAC left state Rep. James Talarico off of its latest list of endorsements for the 2026 midterm elections, the apparent result of a bitter primary contest between the two Democrats that appears to have left lasting scars for Crockett.

Talarico bested the Dallas-area congresswoman in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in March, and Crockett has yet to explicitly throw her support behind her former opponent ahead of the general election.

Crockett started FIRE PAC, which stands for Fueling Individual Rights Everywhere, to help other Democratic candidates win their races. The committee dropped a new list of 24 endorsements on Monday, adding many candidates running for local offices — including county judges and commissioners — as well as state House and Senate races.

Talarico’s omission from Crockett’s endorsement list comes as the state lawmaker, who initially had a fundraising advantage in the Senate race over his Republican opponent, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, has seen that advantage disappear just over a month out from election day.

Crockett’s office and FIRE PAC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
https://x.com/cbs11jack/status/2104531883904172301?s=20It’s not the first time Crockett has snubbed Talarico following her primary election loss.

When asked if she planned to campaign with Talarico last month, Crockett demurred, saying that she “will be campaigning down-ballot.” She also pointed to the issues that arose when the majority of the state party’s fundraising and support went to Democrat Beto O’Rourke, who failed to oust Sen. Ted Cruz in 2018.

“I think that making sure that people that maybe are getting overshadowed because it seems like it’s only about one big race, I think amplifying them, making sure that I can raise their profiles and introducing them to people, that’ll give something more to voters,” Crockett said.

After she lost the Senate primary to Talarico, Crockett wrote in a post on X that she was “committed to doing my part and will continue working to elect Democrats up and down the ballot” in Texas. The two-term congresswoman did not explicitly endorse Talarcio — though the state lawmaker and his campaign welcomed her statement as a show of support.

“I want to push back on the idea that Congresswoman Crockett hasn’t been supportive, because literally the morning after the primary she released a statement wholeheartedly endorsing the whole Democratic ticket here in Texas,” Talarico said on a Houston radio show in July. “And I’m honored to have her support and her endorsement.”

Republicans have held Texas’ Senate seats for more than 30 years, which means turnout across the Democratic base is essential for the party to prevail on election day. Crockett held strong leads in polling among Black voters ahead of the primary, so her support is particularly crucial for Talarico’s campaign.

FIRE PAC’s current slate of endorsements do appear to reflect the congresswoman’s commitment to down-ballot races — though several federal and statewide candidates appear on the committee’s website, including former Rep. Colin Allred, Rep. Christian Menefee and Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove, who are running for U.S. House districts in Texas and California, as well as Xavier Becerra and Rep. Stacey Plaskett, who are running for governor in California and the U.S. Virgin Islands, respectively.

entries.title: Kash Patel’s Top Deputy Abruptly Steps Down
entries.summary: Andrew Bailey oversaw the highly politicized raid on the Fulton County elections department this year, but otherwise maintained a low profile at the bureau.
entries.content:
FBI Deputy Director Andrew Bailey is quitting after just one year on the job, he announced on social media Monday.

As FBI Director Kash Patel’s right-hand man, Bailey oversaw the highly politicized raid on the Fulton County, Georgia, elections department this year but otherwise maintained a low profile at the bureau.

Posting from his personal account on X, Bailey said he was “stepping down to return to my family in Missouri.”

“I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence,” he wrote.

Bailey’s departure comes as the FBI has drawn criticism for prioritizing criminal investigations against President Donald Trump’s perceived political enemies, including former FBI Director James Comey, ex-CIA Director John Brennan and the Southern Poverty Law Center. Patel has taken heat from congressional Democrats over those decisions — as well as the way the bureau has fired dozens of experienced agents who were viewed internally as disloyal to Trump.

Although the FBI director is the face of the country’s leading law enforcement agency, it’s the deputy director who has traditionally handled much of the bureau’s actual day-to-day operations — which is why that role is typically filled by a career special agent who is intimately familiar with the investigative processes and knows how to navigate an institution that is large, secretive and bureaucratic.

However, Bailey’s appointment marked yet another sharp departure from tradition for the second Trump administration. Until he joined the FBI last year, he was known for his willingness to take on culture war issues as Missouri’s Republican attorney general: fighting President Joe Biden’s student loan program, blocking transgender medical care for youths and targeting journalists at the left-leaning watchdog group Media Matters. 

And he came on board as a co-deputy director — another anomaly — to support Trump’s first pick as deputy director: Dan Bongino, a conservative podcaster who’d spent more than a decade as a Secret Service agent but hadn’t previously worked at the FBI.

Bailey drew little public attention during his year at the bureau, except for his decision to oversee the January FBI raid of the Fulton County election headquarters — a government attempt to breathe life into Trump’s widely disproven claims of fraud in the 2020 presidential election.

In June, Bailey discussed the FBI’s focus on breaking apart what he called “industrial-scale scam compounds” during a trip to Thailand. The following month, he traveled to Argentina, seeking to develop more international cooperation in targeting organized crime.

entries.title: Rep. Tom Kean Bucks Trump as His New Jersey House Race Tightens
entries.summary: During a debate, Kean also defended his four-month absence this year as he was treated for clinical depression.
entries.content:
Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr. broke with President Donald Trump on several key issues during his only scheduled debate against Democrat Rebecca Bennett on Sunday night, and defended his lengthy absence from Capitol Hill earlier this year as he sought treatment for clinical depression.

In particular, Kean said that he would fight Trump’s attempts to block funding for the Gateway rail tunnel and that he strenuously opposed the administration’s plan to open an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center in his district.

“I will challenge anybody who gets in my way, including this president,” Kean said Sunday while discussing Gateway.

But Kean defended Trump on the war with Iran, tariffs and the president’s signature tax and spending law, drawing a line between his opposition on the two New Jersey projects and his support for the broader Republican agenda.

The debate took place days after the Cook Political Report shifted the race from a toss-up to “Lean Democratic.” A recent poll found Bennett leading Kean by 5 percentage points, though the difference was about the same as the poll’s margin of error.

Kean and Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot, met for a 90-minute debate hosted by the New Jersey Globe and Rider University in Rahway.

The $16 billion Gateway project would build a new passenger rail tunnel beneath the Hudson River and repair the existing century-old tunnel connecting New Jersey and New York.

The Trump administration attempted to freeze federal funding for the project, but in June a federal judge permanently blocked the administration from withholding the money.

Kean also explicitly opposed the administration’s potential plan to convert a warehouse in Roxbury, New Jersey, into an immigration detention center.

“My focus is to make sure we don’t have an ICE facility in Roxbury,” he said.

The federal government said in June that it had abandoned the project and intended to sell the warehouse. But the Department of Homeland Security reversed course in July and said it was again considering converting the property into a detention facility.

Kean also rejected Trump’s decision to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America.”

“I call it Lake Ontario,” he said during a lightning round.

During the debate, Bennett called for ending the war in Iran and rolling back Trump’s tariffs, saying both are driving up costs for New Jersey families. She also criticized Kean for waiting until the debate to clearly oppose the proposed ICE facility in Roxbury. 

Kean faced additional questions about his nearly four-month absence from Congress, saying he faced a “medical emergency” while receiving treatment for depression.

“We were very clear with our constituents as well as the press that we were seeking medical treatment,” Kean said. “And when things got updated over time, we kept everybody updated.”

He missed more than 140 House votes before returning June 30 and disclosing his diagnosis.

Kean first won the 7th District in 2022, defeating Democratic Rep. Tom Malinowski by 2.8 percentage points. He won reelection against Democrat Sue Altman by 5.4 points in 2024, though Trump only narrowly carried the district by just over 1 point.
