entries.title: Trayon White Says He Is ‘Redeemed Again’ After Judge Declares a Mistrial
entries.summary: The D.C. Council member, who can remain in office for now, was facing bribery charges. The government said it will try the case again.
entries.content:
A federal judge declared a mistrial Monday in the bribery trial of D.C. Council member Trayon White after the jury said it could not reach a verdict, a temporary legal victory for the embattled Ward 8 lawmaker accused of agreeing to help an associate secure lucrative city grants.

Prosecutors alleged that White accepted $35,000 in illegal payments and agreed to accept over $150,000 in kickbacks from a city contractor who, unbeknownst to White at the time, was cooperating with the FBI as a confidential informant.

Within about an hour of the mistrial being declared, U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro issued a public statement saying her office would pursue another trial. The prosecution and defense will meet next month to discuss next steps.

“We have video showing piles of cash being given to a D.C. councilmember as part of a $156,000 bribe. Rest assured that we will retry this case and every corruption case to verdict,” Pirro said.

But White, surrounded by a group of reporters outside D.C.’s federal courthouse, stood firm on his innocence and said the prosecution did not have a strong case.

“I feel like I’m redeemed again,” he said, in a speech stuffed with references to God’s glory. “There was never a quid pro quo.”

The judge’s ruling comes after a nine-day trial in federal court and three days of jury deliberations. The mistrial means that White, who would have been ineligible for public office in D.C. if convicted, can remain on the council — at least for now. His colleagues will have to decide whether to vote to expel him for ethics violations. The council ejected him over such violations in 2025, but White subsequently won a crowded special election to fill the seat he was forced to vacate.

To convict White, the jury would have to have found that he not only accepted the money, but also intended to be influenced by the man who paid him. Prosecutors argued they cleared that bar, while the defense argued the evidence did not show that White intended to carry out a bribery scheme.

Eighty-seven minutes of video, showing White meeting with former D.C. contractor Allieu Kamara, formed the backbone of the government’s case against the lawmaker. Kamara allowed the FBI to surreptitiously record his conversations with White.
Trayon White Trail (5712x4284, AR: 1.33)Prosecutors used the video, along with testimony from Kamara and several D.C. government officials, to argue that White agreed to — and intended to carry out — a bribery scheme in which he would use his position as council member to advance Kamara’s financial interests. They pointed to his outreach to D.C. government officials, in particular the director of the city’s Office of Neighborhood Safety and Engagement, as evidence that he had plans to pressure them to extend Kamara’s grants.

White’s defense acknowledged he accepted the payments, but argued that they weren’t bribes. His attorney told jurors they could have been campaign donations, and said there was no evidence that White actually intended to be influenced by Kamara when he took the cash. They noted that no D.C. government official who testified during the trial said White had pressured them to take action on the grants; the director of ONSE, for example, said White brought up one of Kamara’s companies briefly with her, but never pressed the issue.

By the end of closing arguments last week, the jury had been presented with two vastly different readings of White’s behavior. That disagreement was perhaps no better exemplified by the dueling interpretations of White’s response to the first envelope of cash Kamara handed him in the FBI’s videos.

Prosecutors emphasized the first thing White said as he pocketed the cash: “What you need me to do?” They argued it was evidence that White understood the payment was a bribe.

The defense, on the other hand, used the same clip to argue White was hesitant about Kamara’s proposal. It played to the jury what White said immediately afterward: “I don’t want you to feel like you need to give me something to get something. We better than that.”

On Friday morning, after about two days of deliberating, jurors sent a note to the court saying they could not come to a unanimous decision. Federal judge Rudolph Contreras, who is presiding over the case, told them to keep trying. But by the end of the day Friday, the situation remained largely unchanged.

“We’ve had productive discussions, but have not reached a consensus, and our afternoon vote did not shift from the first vote of the day,” the jury wrote in a note shortly after 4 p.m. Friday.

On Monday morning, jurors sent another note, saying that further discussion had only cemented their divergent perspectives.

Contreras then decided to dismiss them. “I commend you for the extra effort you put and the seriousness with which you undertook this public service,” he said, before telling them they were free to go.

It was not immediately clear how many jurors wanted to acquit and how many wanted to convict. Outside the courthouse, several jurors declined to speak with a reporter about the deliberations.

White’s lawyer asked Contreras if his client could have his passport back. The prosecution did not object.

White gathered with his supporters outside the courthouse to give remarks and answer questions from the press.

“This has been one of the hardest two years of my life, fighting the system,” he said, acknowledging that he could be retried and the case may not be over.

White said he was not gloating — and instead looking at the mistrial as an “opportunity to serve,” a chance to return to the D.C. Council and continue his work. He said he would focus on combatting small business closures in his ward, for one, and added that his experience with the justice system had him considering a return to law school. A reporter asked him, if the $35,000 he accepted was not a bribe, what was the money for?

“Let's stick to the topic, man,” White replied. “We want to accept the jury's decision today, regroup and get back to work, because there's a lot of work to do in this city to ensure equity and inclusion in a $20 billion budget.”

After his speech, White’s supporters gathered around him and prayed. The council member bowed his head and mouthed a silent prayer to himself. As he crossed the street to his silver Tesla, he put a fist up to the sky and pointed to the heavens.

Then he got in his car and drove away, throwing his fans a peace sign out of his open car window.

entries.title: Commanders’ Leo Chenal Will Miss the Rest of the Season With a Neck Injury
entries.summary: The veteran linebacker, who signed with Washington in free agency this year, was hurt making a tackle Sunday against the Seahawks.
entries.content:
Commanders linebacker Leo Chenal will miss the rest of the season after undergoing surgery for a neck fracture he sustained during Sunday’s home win over the Seahawks, according to multiple reports.

Chenal’s brother Adam Chenal posted on X that Chenal was having surgery Monday morning to “replace his wrecked vertebrae with titanium.”

With just under seven minutes remaining in the first half, Chenal attempted to tackle Seattle running back Emanuel Wilson on a 1st-and-10 run play. But as Chenal lowered his head, Wilson’s leg appeared to make contact with the crown of Chenal’s helmet. The fifth-year linebacker then fell to the ground and after a few minutes a trainer motioned for the medical cart to come out.

Chenal was taken to a hospital, and after the game Washington head coach Dan Quinn told reporters that Chenal had feeling in his extremities. While he was being carted off the field, Chenal gave an emphatic fist pump to the home crowd.

Signed to a three-year contract by the Commanders in March following four seasons — and two Super Bowl wins — with the Kansas City Chiefs, Chenal had been thrust into the starting lineup after Frankie Luvu injured his groin against the Eagles in Week 1.

Chenal had 18 tackles on the season, the second-most on the team.

The Commanders (1-2) have few healthy inside linebackers just three weeks into the season. Luvu and Jordan Magee, who sustained a hamstring injury, were both taken out in the Eagles game; Magee was placed on injured reserve and will have to miss at least two more games.

Rookie Sonny Styles Jr., second-year player Kain Medrano, and practice squad members Ale Kaho and Austin Keys are the only available interior linebackers currently on the roster.

entries.title: Work at Dulles Will Close a Runway, Change Flight Patterns Through November
entries.summary: The work will increase the number of overhead flights in communities around the airport.
entries.content:
Residents and businesses around Dulles International Airport can expect to hear more planes overhead in the coming months as one of the airport’s runways closes for maintenance.

Loudoun County officials said in a statement Friday that crews closed the airport’s center runway for planned maintenance and infrastructure improvements, requiring flights to take off from and land at the other two north-south runways at least through November.

Communities north, south and west of the airport, including South Riding, Stone Ridge, Ashburn, Sterling and Brambleton, will experience more flight traffic until the project is completed, according to the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority.

The MWAA says the runway activity is consistent with approved Federal Aviation Administration flight paths and that planes arrive and depart from either the north or the south depending on wind patterns.

Residents who are concerned about aircraft noise can call the Airports MWAA Noise Information Office at 703-417-1204.

entries.title: Contradicting Trump, Pope Leo Says AI Safety Concerns Are Not 'Fake News'
entries.summary: The pope said safety issues raised by AI experts should be discussed and acted on.
entries.content:
By Nicole Winfield

ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE — Pope Leo XIV said Monday that concerns about artificial intelligence going rogue are not “fake news” and should be taken seriously, insisting that safety issues raised by AI experts should be discussed and acted on.

Leo, who dedicated his first encyclical to AI and protecting humanity in its wake, was asked during a press conference about what the United States and China especially should be doing to prevent AI from posing catastrophic risks to humanity. President Donald Trump has called concerns about AI going rogue a “hoax.”

“This is a problem that I think we need to sit down and talk about,” the American pope told reporters returning home from France. “We can’t just sit back and pretend nothing is going to happen.”

Trump has been a champion of AI, often warning that the United States must remain ahead of China in the technological arms race. He has said efforts to limit the technology were part of a “conspiracy” by his political opponents.

Several AI giants, including Anthropic, have called for a slowdown in development to give safety measures time to catch up to the fast-moving technology. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, for example, has warned that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet.

Trump said on Sunday he planned to have a late dinner with Amodei, but he has not yet commented on the meeting.

“If someone were to ask me ‘Am I in panic mode?’ No I’m not. I sleep at night,” Leo said. “I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI should be taken seriously.”

“I don’t think that that is ‘fake news’ as some have said to try and cause whether financial or other some other kind of benefit,” Leo said.

The pope, who called for robust regulation of AI and a slowdown of the technolgoy in his encyclical “Magnificent Humanity,” is up to speed on developments in the field.

Despite being at the end of a grueling four-day trip to France, Leo noted a news report Monday afternoon about Nvidia introducing guardrails into AI. He also noted that the company has previously resisted outside regulation of AI development.

Leo had identified AI as one of t he biggest challenges to humanity within days of his election and took the unusual step of personally launching his own encyclical alongside Anthropic's co-founder Christopher Olah at a Vatican event in May. The initiative was part of the Vatican's effort to engage Silicon Valley about the human costs of AI.

“We need to continue to invite political leaders, leaders of AI, social organizations, associations to come together and look at what is happening already and what could be down the road,” he said Monday.

“To simply say ‘Oh it’s not going to happen’ and close our eyes to it I think is probably not the most responsible way to go about that,” he added.

With his comments Monday about the legitimacy of safety concerns and AI development, Leo has confirmed another area of disagreement with Trump. The two had a back-and-forth in April over Leo’s opposition to the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran and Leo has also criticized the Trump administration’s migration crackdown.

Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping last week in Washington and while Xi said that it was important to ensure AI is “always under human control,” Trump focused more on trying to rebrand it as “superintelligence” and dismissed calls for regulation. However, the two leaders agreed to explore a new “notification mechanism” for AI incidents affecting national security.

AI has become a major election-year issue in the U.S. as some of the country’s largest companies rush to build a national network of data centers while Americans from both parties increasingly raise alarms about the impact on farmland, water supplies and electricity bills.

Worries about AI are continuing to grow inside and outside the industry and reports continue to emerge about increasingly powerful systems that solve problems beyond human capacity but could also go rogue and carry out other, more harmful tasks.

The worries have grown so loud that the CEO of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, said in an interview with Fortune that his company would wait until next year to start selling its stock to investors on Wall Street as it focuses on safety.

Leo noted that ever since he published his encyclical in May, the Vatican has received comments from people interested in being part of a broader conversation about AI. A Vatican commission is working to promote dialogue, study and investigation “to find ways to make sure that AI does not get to a point of destroying humanity or removing humanity from the conversation,” he said.

Leo said he was “relatively optimistic” that solutions could be found.

“I think there are enough people seriously interested in that and willing to look at that outside of the questions once again of power, who gets there first,” he said.

___

AP reporter Roberta Rampton in Washington contributed.

entries.title: Ossoff’s Latest Republican Backer: The State Peanut Commission Chair
entries.summary: Donald Chase joins a growing list of Republican supporters for the Democratic incumbent.
entries.content:
The Republican chairman of the Georgia Peanut Commission says he’s supporting Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff’s reelection bid, the latest Republican to cross party lines in Ossoff’s race against Rep. Mike Collins.

Donald Chase, a bow-tie-wearing Oglethorpe peanut farmer and lifelong Republican, told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution that Ossoff’s support for Georgia farmers had earned his vote.

Specifically, Chase lauded the Democrat’s efforts to preserve funding for overseas food assistance involving peanut-based products. Although those efforts failed to reverse cuts made by the Trump administration, Chase said the senator’s willingness to fight for the industry won his support.

“We don’t necessarily elect a party,” Chase told the newspaper. “I like to support people that I can get behind and believe in.”

More than half of the peanuts produced in the U.S. last year were grown by Georgia farmers, according to the Georgia Peanut Commission, which conducts research and lobbying efforts to support the state’s peanut industry. Chase was elected to the five-person board in January, and is still backing a slate of other Republican candidates on the midterm ballot.

He clarified that his statements were his own, and don’t necessarily reflect the opinions of the more than 4,000 peanut-farming families in Georgia.

Collins’ campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Other Republicans backing Ossoff include Valdosta Mayor Scott James Matheson and Tifton Mayor Julie Smith, who credited his efforts to bring federal resources to Georgia. In Toccoa, the city commissioner and former mayor Gail Fry has also endorsed him, citing Ossoff’s help with funding to replace aging natural gas infrastructure.

Former Republican Sen. Jeff Flake of Arizona endorsed Ossoff as well, expressing concern about Collins’ refusal to recognize Joe Biden’s 2020 election victory.

“Endorsements overall are overrated,” Flake told The Washington Sun last month. “But cross-party endorsements can help and have helped in the past. I think it’s a smart strategy.”

Collins retains the backing of many major Republican leaders.

President Donald Trump endorsed Collins before his June primary runoff against former football coach Derek Dooley. Gov. Brian Kemp, who initially supported Dooley, endorsed Collins this month, arguing that Ossoff’s agenda does not represent Georgia’s values.

entries.title: Trump’s New Rule Could Increase Fuel Costs for Drivers
entries.summary: The new fuel efficiency standards could add an average of roughly $1,600 in costs for drivers, a federal analysis finds.
entries.content:
The Trump administration found that its decision to loosen efficiency standards for new cars could add on average roughly $1,600 in fuel costs for drivers — a higher jump than previous federal analysis suggested.

The Department of Transportation on Monday released a new analysis of the rule revising the nation’s fuel economy standards. The analysis shows Americans should save more on insurance, ownership taxes and other car-related expenses, but would face higher expenses for filling up their tanks.

Under the new rule, which President Donald Trump announced over the weekend, cars and small trucks will need to meet an average fuel economy standard of 34.9 miles per gallon by 2031. Under the Biden administration’s fuel economy standards, that target was 50.4 miles per gallon. In announcing the finalized rule, the Department of Transportation said the change would lower the average cost of a new vehicle by $1,300.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the Biden administration’s standards amounted to an “EV mandate,” and new standards would make cars more affordable and safer, and support auto workers.

“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, we have finally ended the illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want,” he said. “While Joe Biden and Pete Buttigieg pushed a green agenda that made our roads less safe and drove up costs for hardworking Americans, this administration is delivering relief to families and reviving the beating heart of American manufacturing.”

But the federal government’s analysis shows the changes would increase fuel costs for drivers by roughly $1,600. That estimate of how much the rule change will cost drivers has increased even since the rule was proposed; a federal analysis from last year estimated those costs would go up roughly $1,400.

Advocacy groups said the move would add an additional burden at a time when gas prices are rising.

“Families already cannot afford the basics, and now Donald Trump wants to make driving more expensive too,” said Katherine García with the Sierra Club. “Less fuel-efficient cars mean more gas burned, spending more at the pump, and dirtier air in our communities.”

The Sierra Club said it would “fight” the rollbacks, and the Natural Resources Defense Council teased possible legal action over the revised rules.

“Congress established fuel economy standards five decades ago after Middle East unrest led to a spike in oil prices,” said Atid Kimelman with NRDC.” But with the war with Iran driving up oil prices, the Trump administration is doing all it can to keep us dependent on gas guzzlers. In fact, most automakers would not need to make any fuel-economy improvements over the next five years to meet these new standards. This rollback is not only bad policy; it also violates the law. Stay tuned.”

The current U.S. fleet of cars and light trucks already get an average of 35.4 miles per gallon, as of 2024 estimates published in the federal analysis of the rule. That means cars and trucks are already more efficient than the standard the new rules set for 2031: 34.9 miles per gallon.

That’s because the new rules are based solely on gas and diesel-powered vehicles, and don’t incorporate the fuel economy of electric vehicles.

Andy Su, a lawyer with the Environmental Defense Fund, said setting the goal lower than the current fuel economy goes against the agency’s responsibility to set “maximum feasible” goals.

“[The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration] is required by law to improve fuel economy,” he said. “NHTSA’s new interpretation is inconsistent with nearly 50 years of agency practice and the best reading of the statute.”

Su said in addition to increased fuel costs, the new rule could contribute significantly to climate-warming emissions.

“The transportation sector is the nation’s largest source of climate pollution, responsible for 1.5 billion tons of climate pollution every year,” he said. A weaker standard could increase emissions by 1 billion additional tons of greenhouse gases by 2050, according Su’s analysis of the proposed rule.

Automakers celebrated the move. The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which represents companies like General Motors, Ford, Subaru and Honda, said the revision was an “appropriate course correction” from Biden-era standards.

“We’re still reviewing the final rule, but NHTSA made the right call to better align fuel economy standards with the law and current market conditions,” John Bozzella, Alliance for Automotive Innovation president and CEO, said.

Bozzella emphasized the importance of long-term regulatory stability for the automotive industry.

The revision also eliminates a program that allowed carmakers to trade “credits,” which they earned when their vehicles were more fuel efficient than required. Previously, companies could purchase credits from EV companies to count toward their fleets’ overall fuel efficiency.

Carmakers will still be able to earn credits and use them within their own fleets, but under the new rule cannot trade them with other companies. The rule says that could allow manufacturers to work towards more fuel efficiency, instead of relying on credits from third-party EV makers.

The Trump administration has argued the credit trading system has “resulted in a windfall for EV-exclusive manufacturers,” who profit off non-EV manufacturers. Companies like Tesla and Rivian that produce EVs have raked in money from sales of those credits.

The final rule includes a transition period, eliminating the trading program in 2028.

Tesla and Rivian did not respond to requests for comment.

In a reaction on social media, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg said the new rule would weaken the U.S.’s ability to innovate, “handing the clean tech future to China and forcing Americans to pay more at the pump.”

entries.title: Trump Disputes He Asked China's President If He Wanted to Buy U.S. Arms
entries.summary: That contradicts Trump's ambassador who said the offer was discussed.
entries.content:
By Ben Finley, Michelle L. Price And Didi Tang

President Donald Trump disputed that he asked Chinese leader Xi Jinping if he wanted to buy weapons from the United States, contradicting an account from the U.S. ambassador to China.

Trump on Monday acted confused when a reporter asked him about Ambassador David Perdue's remarks over the weekend, suggesting the diplomat was confusing China with Taiwan. But then Trump said “maybe it’s a good idea” to make such an offer to China.

The whiplash over the prospect of arms sales from the U.S. to its ascendant geopolitical rival underlines the Trump administration's often uncoordinated and contradictory approach to China, including Xi's pomp-filled state visit to Washington last week during which Trump appeared to get little in return on key issues.

Perdue, speaking to Shannon Bream on Fox News Channel's “Fox News Sunday” days after the summit, didn’t specify when the offer was made. But such a proposal, if realized, would upend generations of U.S. policy toward China and Taiwan and expose U.S. technology to a potential foe.

China or Taiwan?

The State Department on Monday looked to distance the Trump administration from Perdue's comments, saying that “U.S. law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”

Hours later, Trump seemed to be doing the same.

“To China? You mean to Taiwan?” he said when a reporter asked him about Perdue's account.

“I never heard of that one. I’m going to have to ask him," Trump said.

He then mused that China would probably like to buy U.S. equipment, which he said was superior, and added: “So maybe it’s a good idea. But we didn’t discuss it. He may have been talking about Taiwan. I think he was probably talking about Taiwan.”

Perdue said Sunday that the Republican president was downplaying longstanding U.S. arms sales to Taiwan — which have drawn protest from Beijing for years — by couching it as just one of many sales Washington makes around the world, and even asking Xi if he’d be in the market for U.S. weaponry.

Bream had cited concerns from Republican and Democratic lawmakers over delayed aid packages and weapons orders to Taiwan, the self-ruled democracy that seeks to defend itself from China’s threat to invade the island. Bream asked if the U.S. is denying arms to Taiwan to appease the Chinese president.

Perdue pushed back on the suggestion, stating that Trump “is as strong on Taiwan as I’ve ever seen anybody” and has sold it plenty of weapons. Perdue also said Trump and Xi continue to talk about future U.S. weapons sales to Taiwan.

“But President Trump continues to say, ‘Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,’” Perdue said. “He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some, at one point.”

‘Trump’s transactional worldview'

If so, that offer “speaks to (Trump's) treatment of China in almost exclusively commercial terms, even at the potential expense of the U.S. military position in Asia,” said Evan Sankey, an analyst focused on U.S. policy toward China at the libertarian Cato Institute.

He said the U.S. last sold arms to Beijing in the 1980s and resuming those sales would be “a shocking policy change.”

Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the hawkish think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the anecdote that Perdue told offers “a revealing window into Trump's transactional worldview.”

“He tends to see weapons, tariffs and market access as instruments of leverage, even across the traditional dividing line between allies and adversaries,” Singleton said.

Such an offer to Xi also would come in contrast with U.S. obligations under a domestic law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself and deter invasion from Beijing, which has vowed to seize the island by force if necessary. While not recognizing Taiwan as a country, the U.S. is the island’s strongest informal backer and primary arms provider. But multiple U.S. leaders have left ambiguous whether they would commit military force to defend the island should China invade.

China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a previous summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China.

In their private talks at the White House last week, Xi pressed Trump to oppose Taiwan independence, according to Chinese state media.

In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun did not confirm Perdue's remarks when asked about the matter on Monday. But he told reporters that China has always strengthened its national defense capabilities based on its needs and is committed to maintaining world peace and stability.

This story and headline have been updated to include new comments from President Trump disputing his ambassador's account.

entries.title: Trump Asks the Supreme Court to Back Limits on Transgender Inmate Care
entries.summary: The policy would bar surgeries, hormone therapy and social accommodations for inmates with gender dysphoria.
entries.content:
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to allow its policy limiting gender-affirming treatment for federal inmates to take effect while a legal challenge plays out in court.

In an application, the government argued that lower court rulings halting the Federal Bureau of Prisons policy nationwide pose “security and prison-administrative concerns.”

“Indeed, this Court has emphasized the importance of allowing politically accountable officials to make decisions about the permissible forms of treatment for gender dysphoria, and the need for such policymaking ‘flexibility’ is even greater in the context of prison administration,” the application says.

The Trump administration filing also contends inmates would still be provided “appropriate, individualized treatment for gender dysphoria, while disallowing only interventions that are medically unnecessary.”

The case stems from an executive order President Donald Trump issued in his first days in office that sought to limit gender-affirming care for transgender people in federal prisons and immigration detention centers.

The Bureau of Prisons, which oversees the nation’s roughly 153,000 federal inmates, adopted its current policy in February, barring surgeries, hormone therapy and social accommodations for inmates with gender dysphoria.

In an accompanying memo, prison officials said gender identity “does not provide a meaningful basis for identification and cannot be recognized as a replacement for sex.” The new policy focused instead on providing inmates with therapy and psychotropic medication for gender dysphoria.

Under previous rules developed nearly a decade ago, federal prisons allowed a range of surgeries, hormones and social support for inmates who were transitioning.

A lawsuit filed by the American Civil Liberties Union and other advocacy groups on behalf of three federal inmates with gender dysphoria challenges the Trump administration’s moves, saying the inmates would lose access to medically necessary care.

The suit alleges violations of the Eighth Amendment’s ban on “cruel and unusual punishments,” as well as other constitutional and administrative claims.

In June, U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth blocked the policy nationwide, finding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed at least on their claim that the government didn’t follow required procedures in developing the policy.

The prisons bureau, Lamberth ruled, had not taken into account its “own experience providing gender-affirming care to inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria for many years under its prior policy.”

“The government does not point the Court to evidence that gender-affirming care was ineffective or harmful to its own inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria, or that providing this care previously led to security concerns at BOP facilities,” he wrote.

The judge did not address the plaintiffs’ constitutional claims, saying he wanted to avoid “wading into the culture war being waged against transgender individuals.”

This month, an appeals court declined to put Lamberth’s ruling on hold while the case proceeds.

In the application to the Supreme Court, the government argues that Lamberth should have deferred to prison officials and said they should not have to provide him additional evidence justifying the policy. The district court, the filing said, was “substituting its own policy judgment for that of the agency.”

The ACLU said Monday in an emailed statement that the policy threatened the well-being of transgender inmates.

“The withholding of medically necessary health care, including gender-affirming health care, from people in prison violates their Constitutional right to serve their sentence free of cruel and unusual punishment,” the group said.

The attempt to prohibit gender-affirming care in federal prisons is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to use the federal government to roll back services and restrict rights for transgender people.

Last month, the administration announced a new rule aimed at preventing Medicaid and the federal Children’s Health Insurance Program from funding gender-affirming care for children.

In June, an appeals court ruled that an administration policy barring transgender people from serving in the military was unconstitutional and “driven by the bare desire to harm a politically unpopular group.”

entries.title: Susan Collins Says Challenges to Trump’s Latest Spending Cuts Are Coming
entries.summary: The Appropriations chair is also looking to work with Democrats to put guardrails prohibiting the White House from nixing funds approved by Congress
entries.content:
Sen. Susan Collins, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, told reporters that she is looking at ways to push back after President Donald Trump canceled nearly $1 billion in spending that was approved by Congress.

Trump’s Office of Management and Budget cut nearly $810 million in funds appropriated for health, education and a number of other programs on Friday, just days before the end of the fiscal year.

Collins said Monday that outside groups are likely to challenge the cancellation, which is called a “pocket rescission,” in court. She also said she intends to add guardrails to the next set of appropriations bills Congress must pass in December to prevent similar cuts in the future.

“There are a number of options,” Collins told reporters. “Outside groups may sue, especially since the GAO [Government Accountability Office] has already said that this is not legal under the Impoundment and Budget Control Act.”

Collins, a Republican from Maine, is defending her seat in a “toss up” race, where she has campaigned on her role helming the Appropriations Committee and has increasingly distanced herself from the unpopular president.

Congress is typically able to review proposed spending cuts, but that is all but impossible when the Senate is set to head out of town this week and the fiscal year expires Sept. 30.

Collins noted that although Republicans have previously opposed putting restrictions on rescissions into appropriations bills, she isn’t making “any assumptions” on how her party will react until specific language is drafted.

“We're already looking at whether there's language we can put in the next set of appropriations bills that would prohibit this from happening,” Collins said. “It's going to take some legal work.”

Other Republican senators echoed Collins’ disapproval of the White House’s move in a departure from some in the party’s previous posture on the practice.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota), an appropriator, told reporters that the move by the White House is counterproductive and undermines government funding negotiations, especially as the Trump administration seeks additional funding for the war in Iran.

“It’s going to make it very hard for us to actually get an outcome in the next appropriations bill,” Rounds said of the rollbacks.

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) echoed Rounds, saying that the job of appropriating money “belongs to Congress, not the executive branch.”

And Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said the sudden cancellation of those funds is unlawful, adding, “I don’t think the president has the authority to do it.”

Though Senate Majority Leader John Thune did not go as far as condemning the White House’s cuts, he agreed with Collins that the outcome will likely continue to play out in the courts.

“That again is something the courts probably decide,” Thune said. “Some of these things may be things that many of us agree with. But the process by which they did it is one that is going to be, I assume, subject to a lot of discussion and probably some litigation.”

Democratic appropriators have expressed support for Collins’ call to place guardrails on the sudden cancellation of funds by the executive branch. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois), another appropriator, told The Washington Sun on Monday that he hopes to work with Republicans on it.

“Wouldn’t it be nice if the Republicans who voted for the spending would now stand up and say, ‘This is wrong. We want to restore these funds,’” Durbin said. “It would be nice to have that kind of bipartisanship."

The spending canceled by the Trump administration primarily focused on services for immigrants, including for nonprofit organizations that assist refugees. The White House claims the funds are no longer necessary while border crossings have dropped significantly.

Trump issued such a rescission for the first time in more than 50 years last year, blocking $4.9 billion in foreign aid approved by Congress. The Supreme Court declined to block those cuts.

entries.title: Four Jan. 6 Defendants Sue for a Payout From the Trump Administration
entries.summary: The same law firm filed all four suits, though the claims vary.
entries.content:
Four people convicted in connection with the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol insurrection filed separate lawsuits Friday against the federal government in Washington, accusing officials of misconduct in prosecuting them and demanding compensation in return.

The same law firm filed all four suits, but the claims vary. Two of the rioters, Lisa Eisenhart and Lynnwood Nester, allege the government targeted them for their political views. One other, Peter Schwartz, says FBI agents violated his rights by forcing him to unlock his phone — while a fourth, Kenneth Harrelson, alleges malicious prosecution and false imprisonment. All seek damages but do not specify an amount.

Eisenhart’s lawsuit accuses former Attorney General Merrick Garland, former U.S. Attorney for D.C. Matthew Graves and other officials of malicious prosecution and using the criminal process to punish her for her participation in the riot outside the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. She also says officials violated her First and Fifth Amendment rights through her pretrial detention and conditions at the D.C. Jail.

Eisenhart and her son, Eric Munchel, were convicted for their actions at the Capitol. Munchel, photographed in the Senate gallery carrying plastic restraints, became known online as the “Zip Tie Guy.” Eisenhart was sentenced to 30 months in prison.

An appeals court vacated Eisenhart’s felony obstruction conviction in 2024; her remaining charges were later dismissed with prejudice, her lawsuit says.

Nester makes a similar claim in his suit, which names Garland, Graves and other officials. He alleges the government singled him out because of his political views and ties to the events of Jan. 6. His complaint says eight armed officers arrived to arrest him, despite his lack of a criminal record and the nonviolent charges he faced. He was sentenced to 10 months in prison.

Schwartz’s case centers on what happened during his arrest. He sued the United States, prosecutor Matthew B. Solomon and other FBI agents, alleging they forced him to unlock his cellphone with his fingerprint while he was handcuffed.

The D.C. Circuit later ruled upon appeal that the compelled phone unlock violated his Fifth Amendment rights. It also vacated his obstruction conviction under a 2024 Supreme Court ruling that narrowed the law.

Harrelson’s lawsuit alleges malicious prosecution and false imprisonment after he spent more than two years in federal custody. The D.C. Circuit vacated his judgment in May 2026, and a district judge dismissed the indictment with prejudice in August.

All four plaintiffs received clemency under President Donald Trump’s Jan. 20, 2025, proclamation. Their civil claims have not been tested in court.

entries.title: Drunk Driving Incident Roils the Wisconsin Governor’s Race
entries.summary: The Wisconsin Democratic Party chair received a cease-and-desist letter from a PAC supporting Rep. Tiffany’s gubernatorial bid.
entries.content:
The chair of the Wisconsin Democratic Party received a cease-and-desist letter last week from a conservative political action committee propping up Rep. Tom Tiffany’s gubernatorial campaign, after a Texas man — who had previously worked for a consulting firm contracted by the PAC — seriously injured a bicyclist in a hit-and-run crash while driving under the influence.

The party’s chair, Devin Remiker, issued a biting “public apology” on Friday to Restoration PAC, a super PAC that is primarily funded by billionaire Richard Uihlein, after an attorney threatened Remiker with legal action unless he took down posts on X and press releases from the party linking the man who hit the cyclist directly to the committee.

“For their benefit and to ensure there is no further confusion, allow me to state it again clearly: The individual from Texas who was canvassing to support Tom Tiffany was a CONTRACTOR for Echo Canyon, a firm being paid millions under a CONTRACT, with Restoration of America PAC, which is funded with millions by the Uihlein family,” Remiker wrote in the news release.

Remiker continued to poke Tiffany for allegedly “relying on out-of-state billionaires like the Uihleins to save his campaign.”

According to Wisconsin campaign finance records, Uihlein has contributed more than $3 million to Restoration PAC, and the committee has given Echo Canyon, a political consulting firm based in Phoenix, nearly $2.5 million to canvas on behalf of Tiffany. The congressman faces Democrat David Crowley, the executive of Milwaukee County, in the general election for governor.

Tiffany’s campaign wrote in an emailed statement that the suspect in the crash worked “through a separate outside organization” and “has never been employed by our campaign,” adding that the campaign’s “prayers are with the bicyclist and their family, and the perpetrator should be held accountable to the fullest extent of the law.”

Duan Maiden II was charged with several felonies in connection with the hit-and-run that occurred on Sept. 3. The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported that Maiden admitted to police that he had consumed vodka and four BuzzBallz drinks, ready-to-drink cocktails containing around 15% alcohol by volume, prior to the incident. Witnesses to the crash told police the cyclist had completely flipped over the vehicle, and Maiden was apprehended after a mile-and-a-half pursuit.

Maiden told police in an interview that he had been living in an Airbnb in Milwaukee with eight of his other coworkers while they were canvassing for the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, the Journal Sentinel reported.

Conflicting accounts of the aftermath of the accident began to emerge, especially regarding the timing of a flight for Maiden out of the state booked by Echo Canyon, when the Journal Sentinel reported on statements from the firm and information from the criminal complaints.

The cease-and-desist letter sent to Remiker specifically took issue with the Wisconsin Democrat’s press release alleging that “Restoration and the Uihleins were directly involved in attempting to help Mr. Maiden flee the state of Wisconsin” and the party’s characterization of Maiden as an “employee” of Restoration PAC, because “he was not.”

Wisconsin Democratic Party spokesperson Sam Roecker told The Washington Sun that the party has not received any additional communication from the PAC’s attorney and confirmed that the original Sept. 18 press release and the post from Remiker on X, which are linked in the letter, have been taken down.

Restoration PAC and Echo Canyon Consulting did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

After receiving the letter, Remiker quipped on social media that he plans to repeat his statements about the incident in which he points out that Maiden was a “CONTRACTOR, not an employee, of a firm being paid millions by the PAC funded by the Uihleins.”

“This distinction is clearly very important, and I feel so remorseful that I will repeat this frequently and often,” Remiker wrote Friday on X.

entries.title: DOJ Spent $1.1 Million on Lindsey Halligan’s Security Detail
entries.summary: The former personal defense attorney for President Donald Trump got extra protection in her 120-day stint as interim U.S. attorney.
entries.content:
The Justice Department spent $1.1 million on an unusually large security detail for Lindsey Halligan during her four-month stint as a White House-appointed federal prosecutor last year, according to records shared with The Washington Sun.

Halligan, a former member of President Donald Trump’s personal legal defense team who had no prior prosecutorial experience, received extensive protection from the U.S. Marshals Service for at least several weeks as the interim U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia. She left the role after 120 days because judges ruled she had been unlawfully appointed.

The Sun was the first to reveal the existence of her marshals security detail in October 2025, noting that it followed her everywhere — even as she made her way through the district’s offices. Sources said the detail was made up of three to six federal agents whose constant presence was making employees uncomfortable, given that it hinted at her distrust of career prosecutors whom she purported to lead.

At the time, a source with knowledge about the arrangement said her detail was a temporary assignment and a result of “threats outside” the office.

Regular pay and benefits for Halligan’s detail cost $623,480, according to expense records from the marshals service provided to The Sun by the legal advocacy group Democracy Forward.

The marshals service also spent $191,000 on lodging and nearly $112,000 on overtime pay, according to the records. A “command post” cost roughly $11,000 and rental vehicles cost about $12,000.

Records indicate the detail was managed by the Judicial Security Division, which protects the nation’s federal judges, court officers and courthouses.

Halligan and a spokesperson for the marshals did not respond to requests for comment Monday.

Democracy Forward’s special counsel for oversight, Dan McGrath, called the detail a waste of money given Halligan’s unlawful appointment. “This tracks with the administration’s pattern of wasting taxpayer funds while engaging in unlawful activity as the failed DOGE experiment did last year,” he said in a statement.

Halligan, a former insurance lawyer, was a White House aide before then-Attorney General Pam Bondi in September 2025 appointed her interim U.S. attorney of an office that handles some of the Justice Department’s most sensitive national security cases.

Acting on Trump’s demands to prosecute his political foes, Halligan promptly convened grand juries to indict former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. A federal judge threw out the cases in November, finding that Halligan’s appointment violated laws governing the attorney general’s authority to name U.S. attorneys.

Even after that ruling, however, Halligan continued to act as the district’s top prosecutor and identified herself in court documents as U.S. attorney — a move a federal judge in Virginia criticized as a “charade.”

Halligan left the position on Jan. 20, at the end of a 120-day interim window.

It’s common for the marshals service to assign short-term protection to judges or prosecutors who have received violent threats. But it’s rarer for a U.S. attorney to be guarded like a Secret Service protectee, with a contingent of agents in tow at all times.

The marshals service was already under strain around the time Halligan’s detail began.

The agency logged a significant spike in violent threats to the judiciary in 2025, with many targeting judges who had ruled against the Trump administration in high profile cases. Marshals conducted a near-record number of protective investigations on behalf of judges in the 2025 fiscal year and assigned numerous temporary details to judges and their families, according to agency data and people familiar with the operations.

Around the time Halligan’s detail was running, officials from the federal court system’s policymaking body were also urging Congress to set aside more money for court security, citing a surge in threats. The judiciary’s security budget had been flat for two years. Congress approved a funding increase in the spring.

After losing her U.S. attorney gig, Halligan appears to have returned to Florida, where she had graduated from the University of Miami and is licensed to practice law. In February, she updated the nature of her existing corporation there into a professional limited liability company whose stated purpose was to conduct “legal consulting and related activities.”

entries.title: Homeland Security Rejects NFL Request to Remove Brian Dawkins Video
entries.summary: DHS used the Eagles legend’s highlights to promote its border message.
entries.content:
The Department of Homeland Security has refused a request from the NFL to remove a social media video of former Philadelphia Eagles player Brian Dawkins.

The DHS spot was promoting its message warning about a Honduran migrant caravan traveling toward the U.S. border.

The video plays like a highlight reel of Dawkins’ iconic pregame walkouts and explosive defensive plays, paired with the Korn song “Blind” and coupled with the text, “Our time has come.” It was posted as a response to a news headline about the migrant caravan. Dawkins famously chanted variations of the catchphrase "the time has come" to psych himself up before taking the field.

NFL spokesperson Brian McCarthy told Forbes on Monday that the league had “requested DHS take down the video” after it was first posted Sunday night.

In response, DHS general counsel James Percival posted an image of Bugs Bunny tauntingly saying “No.”

The Trump administration has frequently repurposed NFL, pop culture and celebrity footage into promotional materials to market its policies, and notably layered NFL highlights over military strikes in Iran.

Dawkins, a Hall of Fame safety celebrated for his ferocious, high-impact takedowns, was the linchpin of the Eagles' defense for over a decade. Inspired by the X-Men, he adopted the nickname “Weapon X” and would often crawl onto the field on all fours like Wolverine.

DHS spokesperson Chandler Rebel played up the nickname in a response to Forbes.

“DHS is playing lockdown defense at the border,” Rebel said. “We will use every Weapon at our disposal, from A to X, to keep Americans safe.”

Rebel confirmed that the department was “actively tracking a migrant caravan” but provided no new details about the situation.

The migrant caravan known as "Fe y Esperanza” — which translates to Faith and Hope — has grown to over 600 people since it left Honduras on Sept. 20. The group has picked up individuals from Guatemala, El Salvador, Ecuador and Haiti as it travels north on foot through Mexico.

DHS has issued warnings that illegal crossings will result in arrest and deportation.
